subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Hodgkin lymphoma survivorship, second cancers, ABVD toxicity, relapse salvage and fertility

steps.tx: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (a cancer of Reed Sternberg cells) is cured in more than 8 of 10 patients, so late effects decide long term survival. **Second primary malignancy** (a new unrelated cancer) is the number one cause of late mortality in survivors, ahead of cardiovascular disease in second place. Follow up therefore centres on second cancer screening and heart checks for life, not just relapse watches in the first years.
steps.say: Curing Hodgkin lymphoma is only half the job. Because more than eighty percent of patients are cured, what kills them decades later matters enormously. A brand new second cancer tops that list, and heart disease comes second. That is why survivorship clinics spend more energy on cancer screening and cardiac checks than on hunting for Hodgkin relapse after the early years.

vis.alt: Microscope slide showing Reed Sternberg cells scattered in a mixed inflammatory background in Hodgkin lymphoma.
vis.caption: Reed Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, the curable disease behind survivorship care. Image: Mark Ong, CC BY-SA 4.0.

steps.tx: Second cancers fall into two waves. Early **therapy related AML and MDS** (leukaemia and marrow failure from alkylating drugs, often with chromosome 5 or 7 loss) peak 5 to 10 years after treatment. Late solid tumours (breast cancer after chest radiation under age 30, plus lung, bowel, thyroid and skin cancers) peak 15 to 20 years later and keep rising for decades.
steps.say: Think of second cancers as two separate waves with different clocks. The first wave is marrow cancers caused by alkylating chemotherapy, arriving five to ten years out. The second wave is solid tumours caused by radiation, above all breast cancer in women irradiated young, arriving fifteen to twenty years out and climbing for decades. Each wave has its own screening plan.

steps.tx: Women irradiated to the chest before age 30 carry up to a 30% breast cancer risk by middle age, so **NCCN** (National Comprehensive Cancer Network) advises yearly breast **MRI** (magnetic resonance imaging) plus yearly mammography starting 8 years after radiation or at age 25, whichever comes later. The two tests alternate through the year so the breasts are imaged every 6 months.
steps.say: A young woman cured of Hodgkin lymphoma with mantle radiation faces a breast cancer risk rivalling BRCA carriers, so she earns the same intensive screening. Every year she needs both a breast MRI and a mammogram, starting eight years after her radiation or at her twenty fifth birthday, whichever is later. Spacing them six months apart keeps imaging continuous.

rows: Risk reaches about 30% by age 45 to 50
Alternate so imaging falls every 6 months

steps.tx: **ABVD** (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine) toxicities map to organs. Doxorubicin injures heart muscle (get baseline echocardiography, an ultrasound scan of the heart). Bleomycin scars lungs (get baseline lung function with DLCO, the gas transfer test). Vinblastine damages nerves (numbness, constipation, jaw pain). Dacarbazine causes severe vomiting and marrow suppression with rare later leukaemia, needing no organ imaging.
steps.say: Every student should link each ABVD drug to its target organ, so memorise these pairs. The red drug harms the heart, so the patient needs an echocardiogram first. Bleomycin harms the lungs, so order breathing tests with gas transfer first. Vinblastine harms nerves, so warn about tingling and constipation. Dacarbazine is the vomiter and marrow suppressor, and it needs no special baseline scan.

steps.tx: Hodgkin lymphoma that relapses or resists first treatment is still curable. Give **salvage** chemo immunotherapy (ICE, DHAP or GVD, increasingly with brentuximab vedotin or a PD-1 blocker such as nivolumab) until PET (positron emission tomography) shows complete metabolic response, then consolidate with high dose **BEAM** chemotherapy and **autologous stem cell transplant** (rescue with the patient's own frozen stem cells).
steps.say: Relapse after ABVD is frightening but far from hopeless. The strategy has two phases. First, salvage treatment melts the lymphoma again, and modern salvage adds targeted drugs like brentuximab or checkpoint blockers to reach a PET negative state. Then high dose BEAM wipes the marrow clean and the patient's own stored stem cells rebuild it. That sequence cures roughly half of relapsed patients.

vis.caption: Nodal staging and PET restaging decide salvage and transplant timing. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: ABVD preserves fertility (childbearing ability) with under 5% lasting infertility and no extra risk of birth defects or miscarriage years later, and pelvic (not mediastinal) radiation is what threatens the womb. Still arrange **sperm banking** before cycle one in young men, because a poor interim PET (a scan after 2 cycles) forces escalation to **BEACOPP** (a gonadotoxic alkylator regimen) that causes azoospermia (zero sperm) in more than 8 of 10 men.
steps.say: Couples can be reassured that ABVD rarely causes lasting infertility and does not damage future children, and that radiation aimed at the chest does not harm the womb. Yet every young man should still bank sperm before treatment starts. The reason is the escape hatch: if his mid treatment scan looks bad, we switch to a much stronger regimen that sterilises most men, and by then his sperm is already damaged.
